title: Tamil Nadu PhD Student Makes History at Holyrood
excerpt: Q Manivannan becomes one of Scotland's first openly transgender MSPs, elected on a student visa for the Scottish Greens.
body:
Q Manivannan, a non-binary doctoral student from Tamil Nadu, made history on May 9, 2026, when election results confirmed their seat in the Scottish Parliament — becoming one of the first openly transgender people ever elected to Holyrood.

**What happened:**
Manivannan has served as Member of the Scottish Parliament for the Edinburgh and Lothians East region since the 2026 Scottish Parliament election. They moved to Scotland in September 2021 to study for an ESRC-funded doctorate in international relations at the University of St Andrews. Their election came as the Greens recorded their strongest ever Scottish Parliament result, returning 15 MSPs overall.

**Why this is legally and politically significant:**
Manivannan, an Indian immigrant, does not hold British citizenship or permanent residency, but was eligible to stand for election as a Commonwealth citizen. They were able to contest elections because of changes introduced through the Scottish Elections (Franchise and Representation) Act, passed in 2020 — before which contestants were required to have indefinite leave to remain in the UK. An Indian-born transgender immigrant's election to the Scottish Parliament has triggered a wider debate in the UK over whether temporary visa holders should be allowed to contest elections and hold public office. The Scottish Greens have stood firmly behind their new MSP: the party stated that 'the Scottish Parliament rightly and explicitly chose to permit everyone with the right to live here to stand in elections,' and confirmed that Q holds a valid visa with the right to work and live in Scotland.

**What to watch:**
Scottish Greens co-leader Gillian Mackay told reporters the party would support Manivannan through the visa renewal process, saying 'there will have to be a renewal of Q's visa — that is a process they will have to complete over the session of Parliament.'
